newsitem.title: EGYPT: Middle East peace diplomacy precedes economic talk.
newsitem.headline: Middle East peace diplomacy precedes economic talk.

text.p: Arab and Western leaders talked Middle East peace in Cairo on Monday night in the final hours before the start of a big conference on the regional economy.
But none of them said they expected a last-minute breakthrough in talks between Israel and the Palestinians on Israeli redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat at the Egyptian foreign ministry as the "troika" of European Union foreign ministers prepared for what could be a difficult meeting on Tuesday with the Israelis.
They are all in Cairo for the third annual Middle East and North Africa economic conference, originally called to underpin peace by integrating Israel into the regional economy.
But the election of right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May has cast the conference adrift.

The philosophy now is that Middle East countries must press on with economic reform regardless of political setbacks and that businessmen, rather than just exploiting the opportunities of peace, must add their voices to those of the peacemakers.
"It's a great rally of business leaders for peace," said Klaus Schwab, founder and president of the World Economic Forum, which is organising the event.
"It's not a conference on creating peace with Israel. It's a conference on how to achieve vast regionalisation and how to achieve also the necessary business-friendly environment.
"I think this is a very clear message...that a stable political environment, or in other words a comprehensive peace, is necessary and we expect it to come," he told reporters.
The World Economic Forum said the participants, from 92 countries, include 1,500 foreign businesspeople, 500 Egyptian businesspeople and between 1,500 to 2,000 government delegates.

The agenda covers big regional infrastructure projects, classic economic reforms such as privatisation and trade liberalisation, and a heavy dose of networking by the industrialists and investment bankers who are taking part.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak will open the three-day conference on Tuesday morning, straight after more political talks with Arafat and Christopher.

Two Israeli ministers, Natan Sharansky for commerce and industry and Dan Meridor for finance, arrived in Cairo on Monday night but the head of the delegation, Foreign Minister David Levy, will come on Tuesday and leave later in the day.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, travelling with the Italian and Dutch foreign ministers, said they would probably ask Levy to change policies crippling the Palestinian economy.

"We feel very strongly that there are opportunities in the economic sphere which the Israeli government has not in any way been helpful to. It's very important that these developments are allowed to go ahead as quickly as possible," he said.

The Palestinian business community is boycotting the conference on the grounds that it does not make sense to make business with Israelis when the Israeli government is strangling the economy of the self-rule West Bank and Gaza by closing the borders.
"The reality on the ground is totally contradictory with the objectives of the conference," said Mohammad Shtayeh, head of the Palestinian Economic Development and Reconstruction Council.
Egypt, which in 1979 became the first country to make peace with Israel, has also been ambivalent about the meeting.
Mubarak almost cancelled or postponed it in protest at Netanyahu's policies but eventually decided it would be a good opportunity to attract foreign investment to Egypt.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa tried on Monday to play down the strong Israeli presence. "Israel has been invited just like other states, at the level decided, so we will let things go in a normal fashion," he told reporters.
Moussa and Spring joined others in saying they doubted the protracted negotiations on Hebron would reach a conclusion in time for a signing ceremony in Cairo.
"We have no information about any ceremony in relation to the Hebron aspect of the Oslo accord," said Spring.
"It is not scheduled and there will be no ceremony or anything of the sort," added Moussa.
